title: Human rights and sexual and reproductive rights
blurb: Apply the Human Rights Act 1998 to childbirth: autonomy, dignity, privacy and women's choices about birth and reproduction.
question: A woman with a straightforward second pregnancy wants a home birth. A midwife tells her the unit 'doesn't really support home births' and books her into the obstetric unit. Which right is most directly engaged?

teach.body: SPM 1.3 asks midwives to promote and enable the human rights of women and newborn infants at all times, including women's sexual and reproductive rights. The Human Rights Act 1998 brings the European Convention rights into UK law, and s6 makes it unlawful for a public authority, such as an NHS trust, to act incompatibly with them. Code 1.5 asks you to respect and uphold people's human rights. In plain English: every woman keeps all her rights when she becomes pregnant.
teach.cite: SPM 1.3; Human Rights Act 1998 s6, Sch 1; NMC Code 1.5

rows.label: Justification
values: e.g. protection of health or others' rights

teach.caption: Article 8(2): any interference must be in accordance with the law and necessary in a democratic society for a listed aim.

teach.h: Birth choices are part of private life
teach.body: In Ternovszky v Hungary (2010) the European Court of Human Rights held that the right to respect for private life includes the right to choose the circumstances of becoming a parent, and that the circumstances of giving birth 'incontestably form part of one's private life' under Article 8. Hungary breached Article 8 because unclear law effectively dissuaded professionals from supporting home births.

teach.h: Pregnancy does not reduce a woman's rights
teach.body: English courts say the same in domestic law. In St George's Healthcare NHS Trust v S (1998), the Court of Appeal held that while pregnancy increases a woman's personal responsibilities, it does not diminish her entitlement to decide whether to undergo medical treatment. In Montgomery, Lady Hale added: 'Gone are the days' when a pregnant woman was thought to lose her right to act as an autonomous person.
teach.cite: St George's v S [1998] 3 All ER 673 (CA); Montgomery [2015] UKSC 11 para 116

teach.body: Lucy is a healthy multiparous woman who wants a home birth. NICE NG235 1.3.3 says women may choose any birth setting and should be supported in their choice; for low-risk multiparous women, home birth has lower intervention rates and no difference in outcome for the baby. Booking her into the obstetric unit against her wishes interferes with her Article 8 rights. Her midwife should discuss the evidence, respect her choice and plan home birth care.

teach.h: Sexual and reproductive rights in midwifery
teach.caption: Postnatal contraception discussion supports her choices: fertility can return from 3 weeks after birth.

teach.h: Upholding rights on a busy shift

teach.text: Article 8 is QUALIFIED, not absolute: interference can be justified if lawful, necessary and proportionate. Article 3 is ABSOLUTE: inhuman or degrading treatment can never be justified, whatever the pressures on the unit.

items: SPM 1.3: promote and enable the human rights of women and newborns, including sexual and reproductive rights.
HRA 1998 s6: NHS bodies must act compatibly with Convention rights; key Articles 2, 3, 5, 8, 9, 12, 14.
Article 8 covers the circumstances of giving birth (Ternovszky v Hungary, 2010).
Pregnancy does not diminish a woman's right to decide (St George's v S; Montgomery).
Article 3 is absolute; Article 8 is qualified.

summary: You can now link everyday maternity care to Human Rights Act articles, especially Articles 3, 8 and 14. You can explain why choices about birth are part of a woman's private life and why pregnancy does not reduce her right to decide.

A.q: Which Convention article most directly protects a woman's choices about where and how she gives birth?
A.why: Ternovszky v Hungary: the circumstances of giving birth form part of private life under Article 8.

whyNot.0: Article 2 protects life, not birth choices.
whyNot.3: Article 9 protects religious belief; it may be relevant to some choices but is not the main source.

A.q: Under the Human Rights Act 1998, which bodies must act compatibly with Convention rights?
options: Public authorities, such as NHS trusts
A.why: HRA 1998 s6: it is unlawful for a public authority to act incompatibly with a Convention right.

whyNot.0: Registrants uphold human rights under Code 1.5, but s6 places the legal duty on public authorities.
whyNot.1: Private companies are not generally public authorities under s6.
whyNot.2: The RCM is a professional body and trade union, not a public authority.

A.q: A woman is left uncovered in a corridor in labour while staff discuss her care. Which article is most engaged?
A.why: Treatment that humiliates or debases a person can engage Article 3 (inhuman or degrading treatment), and her privacy under Article 8.

whyNot.0: Nothing suggests she is treated differently because of a characteristic.
whyNot.2: Article 12 concerns marrying and founding a family.

B.q: Which statement about Article 8 is correct?
options: It is absolute and cannot be limited
It binds private hospitals but not NHS trusts
It is suspended while a woman is in labour
It can be limited if lawful and necessary
B.why: Article 8 is a qualified right: interference may be justified if in accordance with the law and necessary in a democratic society for a listed aim, such as protection of health.

whyNot.0: Article 3 is absolute; Article 8 is qualified.
whyNot.1: It applies to public authorities, including NHS trusts.
whyNot.2: Ternovszky confirms birth falls within Article 8.

B.q: Two hours after giving birth, a woman asks the midwife about contraception. What is the most appropriate response?
options: Advise her to wait until the 6-week check
Say it is not needed while breastfeeding
Refer her to the GP after discharge
B.why: Supporting reproductive rights (SPM 1.3) means giving information when she asks. Fertility can return from 3 weeks, and some methods (e.g. implant, progestogen-only pill) can start straight away.

whyNot.0: Fertility can return from 3 weeks, before the 6-week check.
whyNot.2: Breastfeeding protects against pregnancy only when strict LAM criteria are met.
whyNot.3: Deferring her question delays care she has asked for.

B.q: A woman says she is being refused a birth pool because she is from a Traveller community and 'might not follow rules'. Which right is most clearly engaged with Article 8?
B.why: Article 14 prohibits discrimination in the enjoyment of Convention rights, on grounds including race, national or social origin or association with a national minority; here combined with Article 8 birth choices.

whyNot.0: Her life is not at issue.
whyNot.1: Religion is not the basis of the decision described.

C.q: A competent woman at 37 weeks with pre-eclampsia declines induction. A doctor suggests detaining her under the Mental Health Act so that the baby can be delivered. What is the legal position?
options: Detention is lawful to protect the baby
Detention cannot be used to force obstetric care
Detention is lawful if two doctors agree
Detention is lawful if she is over 36 weeks
C.why: St George's v S: the Mental Health Act cannot be used to detain someone because their thinking is unusual, nor to force treatment unconnected with mental disorder. Pregnancy does not diminish her right to decide.

whyNot.0: The fetus's needs do not override a competent woman's rights.
whyNot.2: Two medical opinions do not make detention lawful for this purpose.
whyNot.3: Gestation does not change her legal right to refuse.

C.q: A trust stops offering home births without telling women or giving reasons. A woman who planned one complains. Under the HRA, what does the trust most need to show?
options: That it consulted the local MP
That the restriction is lawful and justified
That other trusts made the same change
C.why: Article 8 is qualified: any interference with birth choices must be in accordance with the law and necessary and proportionate for a legitimate aim, such as safety when staffing is unsafe.

whyNot.0: Political consultation is not the legal test.
whyNot.2: Professional preference does not by itself justify interference.
whyNot.3: What other trusts do does not justify this trust's interference.

C.q: Which statement from Montgomery best reflects SPM 1.3 for pregnant women?
options: Doctors decide which risks a woman should hear
Pregnancy reduces a woman's right to choose
A pregnant woman remains an autonomous person
A consent form proves she was informed
C.why: Lady Hale (para 116): gone are the days when, on becoming pregnant, a woman was thought to lose her right to act as a genuinely autonomous human being.

whyNot.0: Montgomery rejected the Bolam approach for disclosure of risks.
whyNot.1: This is the opposite of what Montgomery and St George's say.
whyNot.3: Para 90: routinely demanding a signature on a consent form does not fulfil the duty.

reteach.title: Rights travel with her
reteach.question: If you imagine a woman carrying a backpack of rights into the maternity unit, which ones does she bring and can anyone take them away?

blocks.body: She brings every right she had before pregnancy: life, dignity, liberty, private and family life, religion, the right to found a family and freedom from discrimination. The dignity right (Article 3) can never be taken. Private life choices (Article 8) can be limited only when lawful, necessary and proportionate, not because it is easier for the unit.

blocks.text: The fetus's needs do not override a competent woman's rights (St George's v S).

explain.body: HRA 1998 brings Convention rights into UK law. s6: public authorities must act compatibly. Code 1.5: respect and uphold human rights.

test.q: Which section of the Human Rights Act 1998 makes it unlawful for a public authority to act incompatibly with Convention rights?
test.why: Section 6 sets out the duty on public authorities.

whyNot.1: Section 3 is about interpreting legislation compatibly.

explain.body: Private and family life covers consent, privacy and choices about birth (Ternovszky). Qualified: limits must be lawful, necessary and proportionate.

test.q: In Ternovszky v Hungary, why did the court find a breach of Article 8?
options: Home birth had been made a criminal offence there
Unclear law dissuaded professionals from home births
A woman was forced to have a caesarean section
Midwives refused to attend women in hospital births
test.why: Legal uncertainty about home birth effectively dissuaded professionals from assisting, interfering with the applicant's choice of the circumstances of giving birth.

whyNot.0: Home birth was not criminalised; the problem was uncertainty.

explain.body: Article 3: no inhuman or degrading treatment (absolute). Article 14: no discrimination in enjoyment of Convention rights, on grounds including sex, race, language, religion and national or social origin.

test.q: Which feature distinguishes Article 3 from Article 8?
test.why: Article 3 can never be limited; Article 8 can be limited if lawful and necessary.

whyNot.1: It is Article 8 that is qualified.
whyNot.2: Article 3 applies to everyone, not just babies.
whyNot.3: No court order is needed for Article 3 to apply.

explain.body: SPM 1.3: women's sexual and reproductive rights: whether and when to become a parent, how to give birth, contraception and lawful termination. Pregnancy does not reduce autonomy (St George's v S).

test.q: From when after birth can a woman's fertility return?
test.why: Fertility can return from 3 weeks after birth, before periods restart, so contraception should be discussed early.

whyNot.1: 6 weeks is the postnatal check; fertility may return earlier.
whyNot.2: 12 weeks is far later than fertility may return.
whyNot.3: Ovulation precedes the first period, so pregnancy is possible before periods restart.
